items.title: Interview: Blue Box Season 2 Director Daisuke Sako on Taiki & Chinatsu Focus and Adaptation Process
items.summary: Interview Interview: Blue Box Season 2 Director Daisuke Sako on Taiki & Chinatsu Focus and Adaptation Process Written by Jorge Manuel Sanchez Moreno Cardenas November 12, 2026 As one of the most outstanding romance stories in recent years, Blue Box highlights the inner worlds and unique sensibilities of its whole cast of characters. The story combines the romantic pursuits of the protagonists, Taiki and Chinatsu, with the passion of spokon , and the adventure of growing up from adolescence. While the Blue Box manga officially ended on July 13 , we can still follow our favorite characters in the anime adaptation currently airing. Blue Box Season 2 explores new sides of the cast and introduces the long awaited Yumeka Goto, a person from Chinatsu’s past. That’s why we were excited to interview Season 2 director Daisuke Sako about Yumeka, the themes explored during the season, and his takes on the story’s message. © Kouji Miura/SHUEISHA, Blue Box Film Partners. Q: Were there any specific themes or core elements you particularly focused on for Season 2? A: This time, we wanted to recreate real, named places as faithfully as possible. The idea that “these characters live in this particular kind of town in Japan” was something we valued in the anime as well. We didn’t only feature the obvious, well-known spots. items.text:
Dans une interview, le réalisateur de la saison 2 de *Blue Box*, Daisuke Sako, explique que la série se concentre sur les personnages Taiki et Chinatsu et introduit le nouveau personnage Yumeka Goto, issue du passé de Chinatsu. Il précise également que l’équipe a cherché à reproduire fidèlement des lieux réels du Japon afin que les spectateurs, qu’ils soient du pays ou à l’étranger, puissent reconnaître ces décors.

items.title: Roundtable: Bartosz Sztybor on Potential Edgerunners Season 3, Retelling David and Lucy's Relationship, and Roman's Personal Inspirations

We talked about the creation process with Studio TRIGGER, how he deals with Cyberpunk ‘s lore, and his insight into Roman, D, Capri, and other characters. Bartosz, who also writes the manga Cyberpunk: Edgerunners MADNESS with illustrator Asano, also commented on the connections between the different Cyberpunk media. Just as in our previous interview about Season 1 , we had a great time talking with Sztybor about the reasoning behind his writing decisions. With his particular humor, he is always open to sharing his thoughts—even at the risk of spoilers. Portions of this roundtable have been edited for clarity. items.title: Bartosz Sztybor and Saya Elder on Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2's Emotional Impact
items.summary: Events Press Conference Bartosz Sztybor and Saya Elder on Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2’s Emotional Impact Written by Jorge Manuel Sanchez Moreno Cardenas November 11, 2026 CYBERPUNK: EDGERUNNERS 2 left no one indifferent after the worldwide release of the ten-episode season on October 20. The latest installment is a new story in the noir world of Night City after the events of Season 1, with a whole new set of characters and ideas on the table brought to life again by Studio TRIGGER and CD PROJEKT RED (CDPR). Following the premiere, Season 2’s showrunner Bartosz Sztybor and executive producer Saya Elder from CDPR flew to the Italian festival Lucca Comics & Games and took part in a special panel on the third day of the convention, October 30, in Cinema Astra. Under the name “Emotional Damage: How Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2 Makes You Feel,” both guests spoke with journalist Eva Carducci about the decisions behind the new season, and the emotions they put into the show. Portions of this panel have been edited for clarity. Beware of CYBERPUNK: EDGERUNNERS 1 and 2 plot spoilers below. Q: How do you make people emotional? Bartosz: Honestly I don’t know. It just happens. What needs to be done is that the creators need to be sincere with themselves. That’s why I always put myself into the characters that I’m creating. It’s also important that when I write stories, they are always character driven. The plot is important, of course. But the character is the most important thing in the plot.
